subtopics.title: Temperature, thermometers and calibration
subtopics.learning_goal: Read and calibrate a temperature sensor; diagnose invalid measurement and defend uncertainty limits.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Distinguish an additive offset from a slope error and select the affine calibration before inferring the sample temperature.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: A linear-assumed sensor displays 8 at a 0 °C bath, 88 at a 100 °C bath and 56 in a sample. A technician subtracts 8 from every reading. Determine whether that model is defensible and infer the sample temperature. A third bath at 50 °C displays 49; discuss the consequence if readings are exact. Shortest valid route: Offset-only would give 80 at the upper bath, not 100. Affine calibration gives θ=100(r−8)/80; r=56 implies 60 °C. At 50 °C the affine model predicts 48, not 49, so exact third-point data refute perfect linearity. Report 60 °C only as a conditional estimate.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Two plausible correction models must be discriminated using both references.

representation_translation.evidence: Coordinates reference pairs with a calibration equation.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Upper-reference rejection precedes calibration and independent midpoint verification.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Third exact reference can invalidate the model.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Construct a common temperature scale from two unequal raw scales, preserving reference locations, interval size and a signed difference.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: Sensor A marks 20 at 0 °C and 70 at 100 °C; sensor B marks −10 at 0 °C and 30 at 100 °C. At one instant A reads 35 and B reads 6. Draw a single temperature axis with both reference pairs and sample points; show which is warmer and by how much. Assume linear response. Shortest valid route: A gives 100(35−20)/50=30 °C; B gives 100(6+10)/40=40 °C. On one true-temperature axis mark 0,30,40,100 and annotate both raw endpoint pairs. B is warmer by 10 K; raw values cannot be compared directly.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Recognize affine calibration rather than raw-number ordering.

representation_translation.evidence: Common axis coordinates two differently scaled raw systems; signed placement is decisive.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Each mapping precedes common-axis comparison and difference.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Raw negative marks do not imply negative true temperature.

qrt_targets.protected_work: Determine whether the claimed accuracy follows from independent reference data, and distinguish resolution, repeatability and systematic error.
qrt_targets.decisive_route: A 0.1 °C display gives 21.4, 21.4, 21.5 °C in a certified 20.0 °C bath (reference uncertainty negligible here), and 51.4, 51.5, 51.4 °C in a 50.0 °C bath. A vendor claims accuracy within ±0.1 °C across 0–100 °C because readings repeat. Justify acceptance or rejection, propose a limited correction and specify an independent check. Shortest valid route: The repeated data are closely clustered but biased by about +1.4 °C at both checks. Resolution and scatter do not bound accuracy. Subtracting about 1.4 °C is a candidate local correction, not a whole-range guarantee. Independently test an unused reference temperature, and report uncertainty/range.

concept_model_selection.evidence: Learner distinguishes repeatability, resolution and accuracy as competing warrants.

representation_translation.evidence: Translate two data clusters into bias and scatter statements.

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Reject claim, identify local model and design independent validation in sequence.

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Extrapolating two checks to a full-range accuracy claim is decisive invalid generalization.

science_records.claim: Thermometry relates a reproducible sensor property to temperature; two-point affine calibration requires a justified linear response.
assumptions: Distinct reference readings and known temperatures
Stable equilibrium, linear sensor response where used
Independent check not used in fitting
conditions_and_limits: Contact thermometer requires thermal equilibrium with the measured body, adequate immersion and negligible disturbance; do not touch container walls.
Two-point interpolation assumes linear response throughout the calibrated interval; two endpoints do not establish linearity.
Scale division and display resolution do not by themselves establish accuracy; extrapolation outside range is unsupported.
Reference ice/water points require appropriate purity, pressure and equilibrium; use known reference baths rather than improvising hazardous temperatures.
science_records.units_and_signs: θ in °C, absolute T in K; differences equal in K and °C; raw readings in declared instrument units.

core1a.phenomenon: Two materials at the same temperature may feel different; a repeatable thermometer may still be biased.
core1a.scientific_narrative:
A metal spoon and a wooden spoon left on the same table may feel different even when they are at the same temperature. Your hand responds to the rate at which energy is exchanged with it; the metal commonly conducts energy faster. Temperature describes thermal state, not the total internal energy or the rate of heat flow. Two bodies at the same temperature are in thermal equilibrium with each other when brought into thermal contact: no net heat transfer occurs. A contact thermometer therefore needs time to reach equilibrium with the sample, and should not appreciably alter that sample.

Thermometers use a reproducible temperature-dependent property, such as liquid-column length or electrical resistance. A digital reading is still the result of sensor calibration. A scale defines numerical labels, and a range defines where the instrument may be used. If 10 degrees occupy five equal intervals, each interval represents 2 degrees; count gaps, not marks. The Celsius and kelvin scales have equal-sized intervals but different origins: T(K) = t(°C) + 273.15. A rise of 8 °C is a rise of 8 K; the offset must not be applied to a temperature difference. Kelvin is written K, without a degree symbol.

For a linear sensor, let r be the raw reading and θ the temperature in °C. At reference baths (θ1,r1) and (θ2,r2), equal changes in θ produce equal changes in r. Thus (r−r1)/(r2−r1) = (θ−θ1)/(θ2−θ1), giving θ = θ1 + (r−r1)(θ2−θ1)/(r2−r1). The offset and the sensitivity (slope) are separate. If the instrument reads 5 at 0 °C and 85 at 100 °C, an indicated 45 corresponds to 50 °C. A third reference tests the linear assumption rather than proving it from the two endpoints. A finer display can still have a large systematic calibration error.

When measuring a liquid, choose an instrument whose range includes the expected temperature, immerse the sensing portion as specified, keep it clear of the vessel walls, wait for stability, and read the analogue scale at eye level. Do not remove a conventional laboratory liquid-column thermometer before reading: it begins exchanging energy with its new surroundings. Repeat readings to estimate scatter; check against a reference to investigate bias. A half-division rounding interval is only an ideal reading-resolution estimate, not a complete uncertainty budget. A clinical thermometer is intended for its specified body-temperature range, not a boiling-water experiment. Use safe digital or non-mercury laboratory instruments under supervision.

derivation_steps.action: Establish a stable reference reading at each of two known temperatures.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Thermal equilibrium and known reference values anchor the sensor response.

derivation_steps.action: Construct normalized fractions of the reference interval.
derivation_steps.why_valid: For an affine response, equal fractions of raw and true-temperature intervals correspond.

derivation_steps.action: Check an unused reference and inspect resolution separately from bias.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Two endpoints always define a line; an unused measurement can contradict the assumption.

model_limits: Contact thermometer requires thermal equilibrium with the measured body, adequate immersion and negligible disturbance; do not touch container walls.
Two-point interpolation assumes linear response throughout the calibrated interval; two endpoints do not establish linearity.
Scale division and display resolution do not by themselves establish accuracy; extrapolation outside range is unsupported.
Reference ice/water points require appropriate purity, pressure and equilibrium; use known reference baths rather than improvising hazardous temperatures.

progressive_examples.problem: A scale has six marks from 10 to 30 °C inclusive. What is the interval? What is the fourth mark?
progressive_examples.reasoning: Five gaps span 20 °C, so each is 4 °C; the fourth mark is 22 °C.

progressive_examples.problem: A linear sensor reads 15 at 10 °C and 45 at 70 °C. It reads 25 in a bath. Infer the temperature.
progressive_examples.reasoning: Sensitivity is 30 raw units per 60 °C; 10 raw units correspond to 20 °C. Temperature is 30 °C.

progressive_examples.problem: A sensor's raw readings at 0, 40 and 80 °C are 0, 23 and 40. Can an exact linear calibration fit all three?
progressive_examples.reasoning: The endpoints imply r=0.5θ, so 40 °C should give 20. The observed 23 contradicts exact linearity; without uncertainty or another response model, intermediate estimates are not certified.

figures.reasoning_step: Distinguish interpolation from an independent check of linearity.
figures.scene_description: Original calibration plot with two endpoint references and a third off-line observation; see Core1A inline SVG.

misconception.wrong_model: A more precise display is automatically more accurate; subtracting a zero offset always fixes a scale.
misconception.diagnostic: Two instruments agree to a tenth on repeated readings but disagree with a certified reference. Which observation tests accuracy rather than repeatability?
misconception.repair: Compare with independent references; distinguish offset, slope, resolution and scatter. Use an affine model only within its justified range.

exit_check.task: A linear sensor reads 3 at 0 °C and 53 at 100 °C; its sample reads 18. What temperature follows? What if a 50 °C reference reads 29 exactly?
exit_check.answer: 30 °C conditionally; the third reading refutes exact linearity.
exit_check.reasoning: θ=100(18−3)/50=30; at 50 °C the model predicts 28, not 29.

core1b.fresh_task: An instrument reads 12 and 72 in 0 °C and 60 °C baths. Its sample reading is 42. A colleague says an offset correction is sufficient. A 30 °C bath reads 44. Assess the model and any conditional sample estimate.
core1b.protected_work: Distinguish an additive offset from a slope error and select the affine calibration before inferring the sample temperature.

stages.predict: Before calculating, would you trust the colleague's correction for the 42-unit sample? Commit to yes, no, or uncertain and your initial reason.
stages.attempt: An instrument reads 12 and 72 in 0 °C and 60 °C baths. Its sample reading is 42. A colleague says an offset correction is sufficient. A 30 °C bath reads 44. Assess the model and any conditional sample estimate.
stages.reconstruct: Offset-only fits both endpoints: θ=r−12 gives 30 °C for the sample. The intermediate bath would read 42, not 44; exact data contradict the offset/linear model. The estimate is conditional, not certified.
stages.diagnose: If you used one correction for every raw value, compare its prediction at both reference points. If you fit two points, check the independent reference. Which observation falsifies your route?
stages.repair: Rebuild the model from both references, then test a measurement not used to fit it; qualify the inferred value if the check disagrees.
stages.boundary_test: If all three bath readings instead agree with the offset model, what changes and what remains untested?

core1b.fresh_task: A sensor reads 2 at 10 °C, 62 at 90 °C, and 32 in a specimen. A 50 °C check reads 33. Select a correction model and report what the specimen data actually justify.
core1b.protected_work: Distinguish an additive offset from a slope error and select the affine calibration before inferring the sample temperature.

stages.predict: Predict whether the 32-unit specimen reading is sufficient to certify a temperature. State your initial confidence and why.
stages.attempt: A sensor reads 2 at 10 °C, 62 at 90 °C, and 32 in a specimen. A 50 °C check reads 33. Select a correction model and report what the specimen data actually justify.
stages.reconstruct: The endpoints give θ=10+80(r−2)/60=50 °C for r=32; offset-only fails the second endpoint. The midpoint should display 32, not 33. Exact data rule out perfect linearity; the estimate is conditional.
stages.diagnose: If you used one correction for every raw value, compare its prediction at both reference points. If you fit two points, check the independent reference. Which observation falsifies your route?
stages.repair: Rebuild the model from both references, then test a measurement not used to fit it; qualify the inferred value if the check disagrees.
stages.boundary_test: If the readings have stated ±2 raw-unit uncertainty, can a one-unit discrepancy alone establish nonlinearity? Explain.

core1b.fresh_task: A scale P spans raw 4 to 44 between 0 and 80 °C; Q spans raw 100 to 180 over the same interval. P reads 19 and Q reads 122. Construct a common labelled axis and compare the samples.
core1b.protected_work: Construct a common temperature scale from two unequal raw scales, preserving reference locations, interval size and a signed difference.

stages.predict: Which sample, P or Q, do you expect to be warmer, or is the ordering uncertain? Record your initial basis before drawing.
stages.attempt: A scale P spans raw 4 to 44 between 0 and 80 °C; Q spans raw 100 to 180 over the same interval. P reads 19 and Q reads 122. Construct a common labelled axis and compare the samples.
stages.reconstruct: P=30 °C; Q=22 °C. Mark 0,22,30,80 in order, annotate the two raw reference pairs; P is warmer by 8 K despite smaller raw reading.
stages.diagnose: Compare your axis with the reconstructed scale: did you compare raw values, misplace a reference, or reverse the signed ordering? Identify the first mismatch.
stages.repair: Map each instrument independently into the same physical coordinate system; then place points and compute a difference.
stages.boundary_test: If Q is outside its calibrated raw range, distinguish plotting an extrapolation from a justified measurement.

core1b.fresh_task: Sensor X maps raw −5 to 15 over −20 to 60 °C; Y maps raw 0 to 80 over the same temperatures. X reads 5 and Y reads 35. Put both results on a single Celsius axis and compare.
core1b.protected_work: Construct a common temperature scale from two unequal raw scales, preserving reference locations, interval size and a signed difference.

stages.predict: Predict whether X or Y has the higher physical temperature, or whether they tie. Give your initial reason without computing.
stages.attempt: Sensor X maps raw −5 to 15 over −20 to 60 °C; Y maps raw 0 to 80 over the same temperatures. X reads 5 and Y reads 35. Put both results on a single Celsius axis and compare.
stages.reconstruct: X=20 °C; Y=15 °C. The shared axis marks −20,15,20,60 with endpoint labels; X exceeds Y by 5 K.
stages.diagnose: Compare your axis with the reconstructed scale: did you compare raw values, misplace a reference, or reverse the signed ordering? Identify the first mismatch.
stages.repair: Map each instrument independently into the same physical coordinate system; then place points and compute a difference.
stages.boundary_test: Relabel the axis in kelvin; what changes about the positions and their difference?

core1b.fresh_task: A probe displays 0.01 °C digits; a stable 15.00 °C reference gives 14.30, 14.31, 14.30 and a 35.00 °C reference gives 34.30, 34.29, 34.30. Defend or reject a claim of ±0.01 °C accuracy and propose the minimum further validation.
core1b.protected_work: Determine whether the claimed accuracy follows from independent reference data, and distinguish resolution, repeatability and systematic error.

stages.predict: Would you accept the probe's advertised accuracy based on these readings? Record your initial judgement and reason.
stages.attempt: A probe displays 0.01 °C digits; a stable 15.00 °C reference gives 14.30, 14.31, 14.30 and a 35.00 °C reference gives 34.30, 34.29, 34.30. Defend or reject a claim of ±0.01 °C accuracy and propose the minimum further validation.
stages.reconstruct: Both clusters show about −0.70 °C bias despite low scatter. Reject accuracy claim; a +0.70 °C correction is tentative in this interval. Test an independent bath and quantify reference and sensor uncertainty.
stages.diagnose: If you accepted accuracy because readings repeated, contrast the observed scatter with the reference error. Identify which claim the observations do and do not support.
stages.repair: Use independent reference residuals to assess bias; distinguish the tested interval from an unsupported whole-range claim.
stages.boundary_test: If the second cluster instead centered on 33.60 °C, what would be wrong with a constant correction?

core1b.fresh_task: A thermometer repeats 40.8, 40.8 and 40.9 in a 40.0 °C reference and 70.8, 70.9 and 70.8 in a 70.0 °C reference. The user concludes it is accurate to 0.1 °C for any temperature. Evaluate the evidence and design a discriminating check.
core1b.protected_work: Determine whether the claimed accuracy follows from independent reference data, and distinguish resolution, repeatability and systematic error.

stages.predict: Would you use this thermometer's displayed value as a certified temperature at an untested point? Explain your initial judgement.
stages.attempt: A thermometer repeats 40.8, 40.8 and 40.9 in a 40.0 °C reference and 70.8, 70.9 and 70.8 in a 70.0 °C reference. The user concludes it is accurate to 0.1 °C for any temperature. Evaluate the evidence and design a discriminating check.
stages.reconstruct: About +0.8 °C bias, small repeat scatter. Reject ±0.1 °C accuracy. A −0.8 °C correction is provisional between tested points. Test another independent reference within the intended range and account for uncertainty.
stages.diagnose: If you accepted accuracy because readings repeated, contrast the observed scatter with the reference error. Identify which claim the observations do and do not support.
stages.repair: Use independent reference residuals to assess bias; distinguish the tested interval from an unsupported whole-range claim.
stages.boundary_test: Would many more repeats at 40 °C alone establish accuracy at 90 °C? Explain.
